film.how: the game’s own replay film: 0–404 s sped up, then 404–422 s at replay speed, ending on “Win at 19:30”

notes.event: AI Tinkerers Doha, Round 5 · Mon 16 Nov 2026 · 15 min, then Q&A

cold.say: [Click once to roll the film. Say nothing for 15 seconds.] This is our game, running in the browser. Our side is Iran. The other side is Brutal, the hardest AI the game has, and it starts with 15,000 extra credits.

ask.say: On the 24th of October our side beat Brutal for the first time, after 39 Brutal games without a win. So tonight, one question: can an AI play our game? Four brains took that seat.

arch0.say: Every brain plays the same loop. The game is the same page as rtsai.net/play. We read only what a player would see: our side, with the fog of war on.

arch1.say: That becomes closed questions: only what is possible right now, plus Wait. For example: which building should we start next?

arch2.say: A brain picks the answer. Three of these are AI models. One is a page of our own rules. This box is the only thing that changes.

arch3.say: The answer becomes the orders a click would send. Every 2 game seconds we ask what to build, every 5 what the army does. The game pauses while a model thinks, a missed answer is played by our rules, and every turn is written down.

code0.say: Here is the whole switch: one function. If the brain is our rules, it is plain code in the same process. Otherwise we ask a model the same questions.
code0.do: Optional: open tools/arena/providers.mjs:144 in the editor.

code1.say: Four brains, four calls: Jev through OpenRouter, Luna on OpenAI’s Decisions API, Gemma on our own GPU, and our rules with no network at all. Each returns a choice and a probability for every option.

prompt.say: This is everything a model reads, every turn. The rubric, word for word: economy first, never leave credits unspent. The battlefield as JSON. And the question, with its options.

rules.say: And these are our rules: a score for each building, right now. The best score wins. About 75 lines like this. No model, no training.
rules.do: Run node tools/arena/provider-smoke.mjs scripted in RTSAI-WebGame: our rules answer a question live.

log.say: Every turn is kept like this: the question, each option’s probability, the pick, how long it took and what it cost. All 64 games, next to their replays.

film.say: Same start, same enemy, four brains, side by side, clocks in step. [Let it run about 25 seconds, then click.]

row0.say: TypeSafe Jev: won 1 of 16, for 8 cents.

row1.say: OpenAI Luna: won none, with 5 draws, for 51 cents.

row2.say: Gemma 4, free on our own GPU: won 2.

row3.say: Our rules: won 9. Free, and under a hundredth of a second a turn.

lesson.say: The hype isn’t what you need. Plain rules won 9; the best model won 2.

turn0.say: Why? One moment. Brutal, start 1, a minute in. Each brain is asked: which building should we start next? Jev, at 1:13: a second refinery.

turn1.say: Our rules, one second later: barracks, almost certain.

turn2.say: Our rules score a second refinery below zero until minute 2. We told every model “economy first”, and Jev obeyed. By minute 3 our army was worth twice Jev’s. Jev lost at 6:44; we won.

why0.say: Across all 16 games: our rules started an army at 1:14. Luna at 2:05, Jev and Gemma at 3:45.

why1.say: At minute 5, Jev and Gemma still had 8,000 to 10,000 credits in the bank. Ours: under 600.

why2.say: So at minute 3 our army was worth about twice theirs. The models saved money and built towers. Our rules built an army.

coach0.say: Fair question: did we just write a bad prompt? So we wrote our rules as advice, and gave it to the models in place of the rubric. Nothing else changed.

coach1.say: And it fixed the opening. Every model now starts its army around 1:14, like our rules.

coachR0.say: The same 16 games again. The three models won 3 between them the first time. Coached: 11. Our rules alone won 9.

coachR1.say: But against Hard and Brutal the models still won none of 24. Our rules won 2 of 8. Better advice fixed the opening, not the hard games.

fail0.say: So how did our rules get good? Not by being clever. On the 23rd, the brain that evening won 4 of 8. Brutal attacks early, so we taught it to defend.

fail1.say: Try 1, early defence: towers first, army home. It won 2.

fail2.say: Try 2, a smarter mix, and try 3, a real bug fixed: none.

fail3.say: Worse every time, and with many rules changed at once, no way to tell which one hurt. So we put the old brain back.

flags.say: The next morning: one idea, one switch. Each switch is one flag in the code, and each plays the same 16 games as the brain without it. The ones that lost stay in the code.

exp1.say: Scouting: none. Budget: none. Counters: 5. Hunt: 5.

exp3.say: Look at the ringed games. Each switch alone lost them; together they won both. One is the Brutal win you saw at the start.

learn.say: Three lessons. Change one thing at a time. Test good ideas together. And rerun it somewhere new: on a map it had never seen, 1 win became 3. Our rules aren’t clever. They were tested, one switch at a time.

voice0.say: So are models useless here? No. This is our voice companion: 281 real orders, slang and misheard words included. Our rules alone read 97.5 percent right. A model for every order: 91.5 at best, and over a hundred times slower.

voice1.say: But rules first, and a model only for what they can’t read: 98.9 percent. The model was asked 17 times in 281. “Train a chilling tank” became the Qilin Battle Tank. And with the rules in front, every model scored the same.

who0.say: Last question: who wrote our rules? This is the git log of that file. 8 commits, every one co-authored by Claude.
who0.do: Optional: run the git log line from the README in RTSAI-WebGame.

who1.say: The loop is simple: read a lost game’s log, add one idea as a switch, play the same 16 games, keep it or drop it.

who2.say: The AI that wins isn’t the one playing. It’s the one that wrote the player. [Stop. Thank you. Questions.]
